name: Autologous fat transfer to face
lead: Autologous fat transfer to the face, also called facial fat grafting or lipofilling, is a surgical procedure in which a person's own fat is harvested from another body area, processed, and injected into the face to restore volume or change contour. For appearance, it is used to fill hollows that make a face look tired or aged, such as the under-eyes, cheeks and temples, and to add projection to areas such as the cheekbones, chin and brow, either on its own or alongside a facelift or rhinoplasty.[1][3][6][15]

Reviews describe the technique as having evolved from simple grafting to finer-particle microfat and adipose-derived stem cell (nanofat) preparations.[2] Plastic-surgery authors describe two long-standing concerns, that part of the transplanted fat is absorbed over time and that lumps can form, particularly around the eyes, and also describe benefits beyond volume such as improved skin texture.[3] Proponents cite as an advantage that the filler is the patient's own tissue, and the portion that takes a blood supply is intended to persist.[15][23]

The published evidence base consists of systematic reviews of case series, a few prospective cohorts and a number of registered trials. A 2017 systematic review of 18 clinical studies covering 3,073 patients found a pooled complication rate of 6 percent and 81 percent patient satisfaction, with the authors noting that the studies were inconsistent and larger trials were needed.[19] Rare but severe vascular events, including blindness, are documented in case series and systematic reviews, and Wikipedia notes that embolic complications are more frequent with autologous fat than with hyaluronic acid.[16][17][18]

In looksmaxxing communities the procedure is discussed mainly as a softer-tissue route to a more defined or less hollow face, and as an alternative or complement to infraorbital implants and fillers.[25][26][27]

paras: Wikipedia describes fat grafting as having three stages: harvesting fat, typically by liposuction; processing it; and reinjecting it into the area to be improved, under general or local anaesthesia.[15] A paper on harvesting techniques notes that many facial plastic surgeons trained mainly in the head and neck region must work on other body areas to collect fat, and details approaches to lipoharvesting for facial transfer.[4] Liposuction itself is described in the surgical literature as a body-contouring procedure that also supplies adipose tissue for lipofilling.[28]

Fat is generally injected as many small aliquots through blunt cannulas rather than as large boluses, an approach reviews associate with better graft take.[24] The 2015 review by Strong and colleagues, which included Sydney Coleman among its authors, examined how harvest, processing and injection choices affect resorption. It reported that donor site, cannula size and centrifugation speed made no significant difference when tumescent solution was used, that centrifuged fat outperformed sedimented fat in patients, and that slower reinjection and placement in less mobile areas were linked to higher retention. The authors concluded that no universal protocol had yet emerged.[22]

Fat grafting is sometimes performed alone and sometimes combined with other procedures. A 2014 description of a lift-and-fill approach integrated restoration of individual facial fat compartments with repositioning of the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) during facelift surgery.[1] A 2023 retrospective study described rhinoplasty combined with simultaneous full-face fat transfer for contour balance in Asian patients.[6]

sections.h: Rationale: volume loss and facial contour
paras: Surgeons describe facial ageing as involving fat atrophy, ligament laxity and descent of facial compartments, which is why newer approaches add volume back, often combined with structural repositioning.[1][15] Coleman and Katzel's 2015 review states that plastic surgeons have learned fat grafting can make an ageing face look fuller and younger, and that grafted fat may also change the quality of the tissue it is placed into, though poor survival and unpredictable results have made some surgeons cautious.[23]

Beyond ageing, the same principle is applied to contour. Online discussion covers fat grafting for the cheekbones, chin and brow area, and as a way to treat hollow or recessed under-eyes without an implant.[25][29][30][31]

Facial uses described in the literature include restoring volume lost with ageing, contouring, and treatment of the periorbital region.[1][3][15] Related cosmetic applications include rejuvenation of the back of the hand, where reviews describe restoring subcutaneous fat to soften prominent veins and tendons and report high patient satisfaction.[32] Wikipedia also lists rhinoplasty adjuncts, for example for a low dorsum.[15]

A 2025 comparative trial reported in the dermatology literature examined fat enriched with adipose-derived stem cells for post-acne depressed spots on the face, a use in which localized fat atrophy is the target.[33]

Registered studies include fat grafting in facial atrophy, craniofacial microsomia, post-burn facial scars and HIV-associated lipodystrophy, indicating use beyond purely cosmetic goals.[7][8][9][10][13] A prospective cohort of 20 patients with craniofacial deformities from trauma or surgery, published in the Annals of Surgery in 2021, reported no serious adverse events and improved patient-rated satisfaction with physical appearance and social functioning at 9 months.[21]

Published literature is largely narrative reviews, surgeon-reported series and a small number of prospective studies rather than large controlled trials. Review articles discuss microfat and nanofat grafting, long-term sequelae, and harvesting techniques.[2][3][4] A 2020 review covers autologous facial fat transfer as soft-tissue augmentation and regenerative therapy.[5]

A 2017 systematic review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open (Groen and colleagues) searched through December 2016 and included 18 clinical articles covering 3,073 patients, with mean follow-up of 13.9 months. The pooled complication rate was 6 percent; the most frequent complications were hematoma or bruising (5 percent), fat necrosis or oil cysts (2 percent), irregular fat distribution (2 percent) and scarring (2 percent). No major complications were reported and overall patient satisfaction was 81 percent. The authors described the evidence as limited and inconsistent and called for larger multicenter randomized trials using volumetric measurement.[19]

A 2021 prospective cohort (Bourne and colleagues, including Coleman and Rubin) measured retention by high-resolution CT in 20 craniofacial patients. Average retention at 9 months was 63 percent; retention at 3 months strongly predicted retention at 9 months; injected volume did not correlate with retention; and age, sex and BMI had no effect, while former smokers unexpectedly retained more than non-smokers.[21]

A 2022 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal looked at supplements added to facial fat grafts to improve retention: platelet-rich plasma, platelet-rich fibrin, adipose- or bone marrow-derived stromal cells, stromal vascular fraction and nanofat. Of 27 included studies, volume retention improved in 13 of 22 that measured it and satisfaction was higher in 5 of 16; study quality was weak in 20 of 27, and the authors concluded it remained unclear whether additives improve retention.[20]

Registered clinical studies include a phase 2 study of adipose-derived stem cells in facial fat grafting for facial atrophy (NCT02526576, 34 participants, completed), a phase 2 trial of fat grafts supplemented with adipose-derived regenerative cells in craniofacial microsomia (NCT01674439, 29 participants), a study of psychological morbidity and facial volume in HIV lipodystrophy (NCT01359917, 50 participants), and a small terminated study of concentrating stromal cells in fat grafts (NCT01564524).[7][8][9][10] Other registered studies examine facial skin quality after lipofilling (NCT07737639), a processing system (NCT05522426, not yet recruiting) and a device-assisted grafting technique (NCT06169670, 11 participants).[11][12][14] A registered comparison of fat injection with platelet-rich plasma for post-burn facial scars (NCT04557514) also exists.[13]

A frequently cited limitation is that a share of the grafted fat is reabsorbed. Wikipedia reports that up to half may be reabsorbed in breast augmentation, and that weight gain or loss can alter results since transferred fat behaves like fat elsewhere in the body; survival is described as dependent on gentle handling and prompt reinjection.[15] Facial plastic-surgery authors discuss perceived absorption and dissipation as one of two main problems limiting wider acceptance.[3] The 2021 craniofacial cohort measured about 63 percent retention at 9 months, with volume stable from about 3 months.[21]

Reviews of technique note that resorption is unpredictable because many variables in harvesting, processing and injection affect results, and that repeat sessions with small volumes are favoured by many surgeons.[22][24] Proponents of microfat and nanofat techniques describe them as attempts to overcome early limitations, and some papers describe added skin-texture improvement.[2][3]

Wikipedia lists swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain or altered sensation, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities, injury from the cannula and fat necrosis as possible complications.[15] A review of limitations and long-term sequelae highlights lumps and bulges, particularly in the periorbital region.[3] A 2017 review describes complications as generally minor, including bruising, swelling, pain, infection, necrosis and calcification.[24]

Retinal artery occlusion and blindness from retrograde embolization are rare but serious events described for facial fillers in general, and Wikipedia states that embolic complications are more frequent with autologous fat than with hyaluronic acid.[16] A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of ophthalmic complications after facial fat injection included 34 articles from 1,052 publications; periorbital swelling was the most common first symptom, the forehead the most frequent injection site, and ophthalmic artery occlusion had a pooled prevalence of about 50 percent. The authors concluded the procedure is generally safe in cosmetic use but that serious outcomes including blindness occur.[17]

A 2023 systematic review of arterial embolism after facial fat grafting identified 61 patients (mean age about 34). The glabella, multiple facial regions and the temples were the most common injection sites; visual symptoms were the most frequent presentation; every patient with ophthalmic artery occlusion had permanent vision loss, and six patients died. The authors noted the lack of high-quality data and recommended a case database.[18]

Fat is often compared with hyaluronic acid filler and with solid implants. Wikipedia notes that the FDA regulates manufactured fillers as medical devices in the United States.[16] Fat differs in being the patient's own tissue, requiring a harvest site and a surgical procedure, and having variable persistence.[15][22] The 2017 systematic review concluded fat appeared promising, with fewer complications than other fillers and high satisfaction, while calling for better trials.[19]
For under-eye hollows, the comparison in community discussion is usually between fat, filler and infraorbital implants, weighing downtime, cost, reversibility and predictability.[25][27][31]

On looksmax.org, threads discuss fat grafting for the cheekbones, chin, brow ridge, under-eyes and lower-lid support, asking how it works, how it compares with fillers and implants, and what to know beforehand.[26][29][30][31][34][35] One poster weighing options for recessed under-eyes described fat grafting as the next-best option after implants but less predictable than filler or implants and not reversible, with a worry about looking puffy; the same post described filler as fast and cheap but prone to migration.[25]

Another thread asks whether fat grafting is effectively a permanent alternative to fillers and implants, and another asks whether implants are worth the money compared with under-eye fat grafting or filler.[26][27] Users also discuss grafting over existing implants, where replies state the infection risk is not high but greater with silicone.[36] Do-it-yourself fat grafting has also been discussed on forums; the wiki does not provide instructions, and the harvest and injection steps are described in the medical literature as surgical procedures.[15]

timeline.event: Review of limitations, complications and long-term sequelae of facial fat transfer published in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics of North America.[3]
Paper on fat harvesting techniques for facial fat transfer published; a phase 2 trial of fat grafts with adipose-derived regenerative cells in craniofacial microsomia begins.[4][8]
Lift-and-fill facelift integrating fat compartment restoration described in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[1]
Coleman and Katzel publish a review of fat grafting for facial filling and regeneration; Strong and colleagues review harvesting, processing and injection techniques.[22][23]
Groen and colleagues publish a systematic review of 18 studies and 3,073 patients on autologous fat transfer for facial rejuvenation.[19]
Review of microfat and nanofat techniques published.[2]
Prospective cohort measures CT-based fat retention of about 63 percent at 9 months in craniofacial patients.[21]
Systematic reviews of ophthalmic complications after facial fat injection and of retention-boosting supplements published.[17][20]
Systematic review of arterial embolism after facial fat grafting identifies 61 patients; rhinoplasty with full-face fat transfer study published.[6][18]

lore.intro: Facial fat grafting is discussed on looksmax.org and in related communities as a natural-tissue option for under-eye hollows, cheeks, chin and brow, usually in comparison with filler and implants.[25][26][27]

claims.claim: Fat grafting is a near-permanent alternative to fillers and implants
claims.believers: Posters ask whether fat that survives behaves as permanent living tissue and so replaces repeated filler or implants.[26]
claims.experts: Surgical reviews describe part of the graft as reabsorbed and retention as variable; one 9-month CT cohort measured about 63 percent retention that stabilised by 3 months.[3][21]

claims.claim: Fat grafting is less predictable than filler or implants for the under-eyes
claims.believers: One poster described it as less predictable than filler or implants, not reversible, and with a chance of looking puffy.[25]
claims.experts: Facial plastic-surgery authors name lumps and bulges around the eyes as a main problem; a 2017 review found a 6 percent pooled complication rate.[3][19]

claims.claim: Adding PRP, stem cells or nanofat improves graft survival
claims.believers: Surgeons and patients describe stem-cell-enriched or nanofat preparations as ways to improve retention and skin quality.[2]
claims.experts: A 2022 systematic review found retention improved in 13 of 22 studies, with weak study quality in 20 of 27, and concluded it remained unclear.[20]

claims.claim: Fat can be added over existing implants
claims.believers: Replies in one thread state it can be done, with infection risk not high but greater over silicone.[36]
claims.experts: No controlled studies on grafting over facial implants were located.

claims.claim: Fat grafting is a low-risk procedure
claims.believers: Proponents cite the use of the patient's own tissue, and a 2017 review characterised fat grafting as a low-risk way to correct soft-tissue defects.[24]
claims.experts: Reviews describe mostly minor complications, while systematic reviews document rare embolic vision loss, stroke and deaths after facial fat injection.[17][18][24]

claims.claim: Fat grafting can improve skin quality as well as volume
claims.believers: Proponents of microfat and nanofat describe better skin texture and tone.[2][3]
claims.experts: Reviews mention texture benefits as a derivative effect; registered studies of skin-quality change after lipofilling are small.[3][11]

claims.claim: Fat grafting can contour the cheekbones, chin and brow
claims.believers: Threads discuss grafting for zygomatic projection, chin augmentation and brow ridge as alternatives to implants.[29][30][31]
claims.experts: Published facial series focus mainly on volume restoration and rejuvenation; a retrospective study reports full-face transfer combined with rhinoplasty for contour balance.[6]

card.summary: Using your own harvested fat as a face filler; well-established surgical technique, with variable retention and rare serious complications.
card.note: Part of the fat may be reabsorbed; rare vascular complications including vision loss are described.

quick.overview:
Facial fat transfer takes fat from elsewhere on your body and places it in the face to restore volume or change contour. Surgeons use it in facelifts, for hollow areas, and in reconstructive cases.

Most published material is narrative reviews and surgeon-reported technique, with some small registered trials of stem-cell enriched fat and processing devices.
quick.mechanism: Fat is collected by liposuction, processed, and injected as small amounts into target areas. Some of it survives as living tissue and some is absorbed; newer microfat and nanofat methods use finer preparations, partly for skin quality.
quick.risks: Reported problems include swelling, bruising, lumps or contour irregularities, donor-site issues and fat necrosis. Rare embolic events including blindness have been described, and Wikipedia reports these are more frequent with fat than with hyaluronic acid. Retention varies from person to person.

chain: Fat is harvested from the body, usually by liposuction
Processed fat is injected in small amounts into hollow or flat facial areas
The surviving fat fills hollows and adds projection, giving a fuller, smoother, more defined face
angle.text: People use facial fat transfer to fill under-eye hollows, cheeks and temples and to add support to the chin, cheekbones or brow so that the face reads as fuller, smoother or better balanced. The result comes from the portion of the grafted fat that takes a blood supply and persists; surgeons also describe finer microfat and nanofat preparations used for skin quality.[2][3][15][21]
